definition: Bardo (Bardo Thodol) in PKD's exegesis is the post-mortem intermediate state described in the Tibetan Book of the Dead, which PKD read as a template for his own experience before and during 2-74 and as the narrative matrix he adapted in writing *Ubik*, inserting a Logos-like rescuing presence that the source text does not contain. The Bardo trip ends when the cycle of rebirths closes and the soul returns to God — the meaning PKD assigned to the bright white light.
interpretive_note: PKD identifies his 2-74 experience as a Bardo Thodol trip that culminated in rebirth — resurrection — returning him in consciousness to the era of Acts. He reads the Bardo state as characterised by an irrational, irreal maze in which characters are hurled helplessly through projections of their own thoughts, while Valis remains rational and present but invisible to them — the condition *Ubik* dramatizes. His composition of *Ubik* was itself an experimental engagement with the Bardo Thodol: he followed the journey's structure and then deliberately departed from it by adding Ubik, a vast Logos-like mind that invades the decaying bardo world and rescues its inhabitants. A separate speculation entertains the possibility that the post-Bardo celestial-wholeness state — normally triggered by physical death — fired prematurely in PKD through some anti-karmic intervention, though this reading remains tentative. PKD also connects the Bardo's structure to the Greco-Roman mystery religions, all of which, in his reading, aim to free the initiate from astral determinism, just as the Bardo journey aims to free the soul from rebirth.
